content: The CDX1 protein, also known as Homeobox protein CDX-1, is a protein in humans encoded by the CDX1 gene. This protein is expressed in the developing endoderm and continues to be expressed in the intestine throughout adulthood. The expression of CDX1 protein varies along the intestine, with high levels observed in intestinal crypts and progressively lower levels along the intestinal villi. The CDX1 gene belongs to the caudal-related homeobox transcription factor family. The protein it encodes is a DNA-binding protein that regulates intestine-specific gene expression and plays a role in the differentiation of enterocytes. CDX1 has been shown to induce the expression of the intestinal alkaline phosphatase gene and inhibit the transcriptional activity of the beta-catenin/T-cell factor pathway. Additionally, CDX1 plays a significant role in embryonic epicardial development. Research has demonstrated that CDX proteins suppress cardiac differentiation in both zebrafish and mouse embryonic stem cells, although the precise mechanisms underlying this process remain poorly understood. Transient expression of CDX1 around five days post-coitum (dpc) is thought to promote epicardial epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), which is essential for proper cardiovascular development. Low-dose induction of CDX1 has been shown to enhance the migration and differentiation of epicardium-derived cells into vascular smooth muscle cells. In contrast, sustained high-dose induction of CDX1 or a deficiency in CDX1 impairs the ability of these cells to migrate and differentiate into smooth muscle cells, a process mediated by TGF-β1. Furthermore, CDX1 induction alters the transcript expression of genes involved in cell adhesion, EMT, and angiogenesis. In addition to its established roles in intestinal patterning and differentiation, CDX1 has been demonstrated to be critical for epicardial development.
